title: A scroll without vowels
hookLine: twenty-two letters, no vowels on the scroll: the reader brings the breath
carry: the torah's letters wait for a living voice

cards: Open Psalm one hundred nineteen in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, and odd headings interrupt the poem. Aleph. A stretch of verses.
Daleth. A strange word over every section. In English it's easy to skip them.
In Hebrew you can't, because in each section every line begins with that letter.

teach.b: Alef-bet: the Hebrew alphabet, named for its first two letters, alef and bet. You first met it in year one, with the man who knew no prayers and said the letters instead. Turn it four ways.
First, the count. Count that psalm's headings, from Aleph to Tav: there are twenty-two.
Other poems in the Bible are built the same way, like the woman of valor at the end of Proverbs, each line starting with the next letter. The alphabet becomes a frame for praise.

Second, all consonants. Every one of the twenty-two is a consonant; no letter is simply a vowel, the way a or e is in English. Vowels, when they're shown, are small dots and dashes under, over and beside the letters.
Third, the scroll. A Torah scroll is written with the letters alone, no vowel marks at all.

The reader has to know how the words sound, so a child preparing to read from the Torah practices from a printed book with the vowels in, then reads from the scroll without them. Fourth, why it matters.
Some teachers picture the letters as a body and the vowels as the breath that moves it.
On the parchment the breath is missing, and the reader brings it.
Every time the Torah is read aloud, a living voice supplies what the ink can't.

how: Jewish children learn the twenty-two letters of the alef-bet, all consonants, and then the vowel marks; a Torah scroll is written without vowels, so readers prepare from a printed text before chanting from the scroll.

practice: You'll hear the twenty-two names once; say them after, softly, or just listen: alef, bet, gimel, dalet, hey, vav, zayin, chet, tet, yod, kaf, lamed, mem, nun, samech, ayin, pey, tsadi, kuf, resh, shin, tav.
You don't need to remember them all; notice which one stuck, maybe the first, maybe shin from yesterday. If you pray, some of these sounds are already in your prayers.
